title: Nature Restoration Law

definition.text: A 2024 European Union regulation that makes binding targets for restoring damaged nature across the EU.

facts.text: Member states must restore at least 30% of habitats in poor condition by 2030, 60% by 2040 and 90% by 2050.
It responds to more than 80% of Europe's habitats being in poor condition.
Its aims include protecting ecosystem services, mitigating climate change and reducing risks to food security.
Farm groups and the European People's Party opposed it as a threat to livelihoods; the Parliament passed it 329 to 275 and it took effect on 18 August 2024.

contested_note: Farming groups and centre-right parties opposed it as harmful to farmers, while scientists and the IUCN backed it.
notes: EU-level regulation kept as a regional example of binding restoration targets; drop if the course excludes regional laws.

definition.text: An international treaty, signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, for the conservation and wise use of wetlands of international importance.

facts.text: It took effect on 21 December 1975 and is also called the Convention on Wetlands.
In February 2025 its list held 2,531 Ramsar sites covering over 2.6 million square kilometres.
To join, a country had to designate at least one wetland site and guarantee its protection.
World Wetlands Day, 2 February, marks its adoption in 1971.
Domestic implementation is often half-hearted and inadequate.

title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
article: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

definition.text: An international treaty, known as UNCLOS, that sets the legal framework for all marine and maritime activities.

facts.text: It came out of the third UN Conference on the Law of the Sea, 1973 to 1982, and entered into force on 16 November 1994.
It replaced the 17th-century 'freedom of the seas' idea, under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation.
It set zones measured from a baseline, including exclusive economic zones extending 200 nautical miles.
Part XI created the International Seabed Authority to license seabed mining and distribute royalties.
Part XII obliges all states to cooperate in protecting the marine environment.
It has 172 parties; the United States signed but has not ratified it.
The 2023 High Seas Treaty was added because UNCLOS gave no framework for biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction.

title: Exclusive economic zone

definition.text: A sea area, set by the Law of the Sea convention, where a coastal state has exclusive rights to explore and use marine resources.

facts.text: It stretches from 12 to 200 nautical miles from the coast.
EEZs were introduced to end heated clashes over fishing rights, as oil also grew important.
EEZs cover about one-third of the ocean; the other two-thirds lie beyond national jurisdiction.

prerequisites: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

title: Common heritage of mankind

definition.text: The principle that certain resources, such as the deep seabed, belong to all humanity rather than to any one nation.

facts.text: Plant genetic resources were treated as common heritage before the CBD and could be freely exchanged for breeding and research.
Developing countries criticised this approach because their resources could be exploited without compensation; the CBD replaced it with national sovereignty.
High Seas Treaty talks turned on the contrast between 'freedom of the seas' and 'common heritage of mankind'.

prerequisites: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
contested_note: Developing countries and industrialised nations disagree over whether genetic resources should be common heritage or sovereign property.
